title: Pronouncing Bigard and Villere; Creole and American New Orleans
summary: He explains the American versus patois pronunciations and that Canal Street divided the American section from the French-speaking Creole section, who rarely mixed.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: You see, in New Orleans, naturally the American people say Bigard, but in New Orleans' patois they call it Bigard.
That's half French -- a piece of French and whatever. It's Bigard.
And my whole name is Albade Leon Bigard.
Which sounds very French, but yet,--
-- on the other hand, you pronounced the name of the street where you were born --
-- Villere rather than the French pronunciation.
That's the only pronunciation for that street, is Villere.
Oh, I see. So there were both French pronunciation and Americanized pronunciation for French words, in New Orleans.

Yeah. Well, the American -- they never used it -- You see, like New Orleans was divided. Canal Street divided -- they used to say the American part of Louisiana and from American down was the Creole section, which was the half French. You know, the patois French.
And that's the way it was, and so they never really got together too much.
